# Garry Kasparov: Concise Summary
Garry Kasparov, born Garik Kimovich Weinstein in Baku in 1963, rapidly rose through the chess world, becoming the youngest ever world No. 1 in 1984 and the youngest ever World Chess Champion in 1985 after defeating Anatoly Karpov. Kasparov retained his world champion status for 15 years, engaging in five legendary title matches against Karpov. He broke away from FIDE in 1993, forming the Professional Chess Association and continued to dominate top-level chess until his retirement from regular competition in 2005, while maintaining the world No. 1 ranking. Kasparov was renowned for his dynamic tactical style, deep preparation, and innovations in chess opening theory, setting Elo rating records and winning most major tournaments he entered for over a decade.
Post-retirement, Kasparov participated in exhibition matches, contributed to chess education and technology, and coached elite players including Magnus Carlsen. He played notable matches against chess computers, including his historic loss to IBM's Deep Blue in 1997. Kasparov authored many influential chess books, including the multi-volume "My Great Predecessors" series, and developed chess platforms and instructional video content. Beyond chess, Kasparov became a prominent Russian opposition activist, founding the United Civil Front, helping lead The Other Russia coalition, and speaking out against Vladimir Putin. He participated in election campaigns, ran for FIDE president, and has been active internationally in human rights and political commentary. Kasparov now resides in New York, continues to write, and is engaged in political advocacy, particularly in support of democracy and against authoritarianism in Russia.
